utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber received this morning a filing from the Office of the Prosecution in relation to self-representation. Would we expect also any written submissions, or would you -- Mr. Stewart, will you limit yourself to oral submissions? We did not invite for written submissions, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, you didn't invite and we didn't respond to the invitation that wasn't given. No, Your Honour, and we're not proposing -- I received the -- I've got these the wrong way round, I think. I received the Prosecution's submissions this morning when I got back from the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the practical terms, responding in writing, anyway, is not an option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No, I do understand. But at least it's good to know that you received it, and, of course, there was not that much time still to read it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have read it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, so did the Chamber. Yes. Then I'm also informed that there's still a filing to be expected rather soon, and perhaps the parties could at least see whether at the next break there would be such a filing, which would be a filing by the Registry on the subject. As you all know that the Registry is entitled to make whatever filing they'd like under Rule, what is it, 33, I think it is. Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar points me to Rule 33(B), which reads that "The Registrar in the execution of his or her functions may make oral and written representations to the President or Chambers on any issue arising in the context of a specific case which effects or may effect the discharge of such functions." And that's not even the whole of it, but notice to the parties should be given where necessary. So, therefore, if the Registry has not yet given notice -- they couldn't do it because there was no filing yet, but this already draws the attention of the parties to the possibility that there would be such a filing. Then if there's no other procedural issue to be raised, I'd like to return into closed session in order to hear the remainder of the cross- examination of Witness 665.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I just wonder whether I should inquire if there's any information when we're going to get this filing in view of the imminence of this issue being dealt with, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There are going to be limited opportunities to read it, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the Registry takes a specific position; they can file whenever they want as long as it is within the ambit of Rule 33(B). But since it might be of importance, I take it, Madam Registrar, that as soon as it has been filed, that notice and a copy will be given immediately to those interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, I suppose the Registry appreciate the importance of filing something before the issue that it's directed to is actually resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- well, thank you, Your Honours. We've -- if we could, because I may be able to at least get somebody to look at it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- straight away. I'm not quite sure who will be lucky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar informs me that the filing would be within the next hour or hour and a half. Then we could return into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see that you are now replaced by Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next issue on the agenda is the letter written by Mr. Krajisnik and sent to the Registrar in which he expresses that he wants to defend himself for, as I understand, the remainder of the trial. Last week we have paid some attention to it. The Chamber is aware that you, Mr. Stewart, have written a letter to the Registrar explaining your position. The Chamber has given what I would call a provisional ruling last week, that we still first have to hear further submissions, and we have to further determine what the effect would be of the letter written by Mr. Krajisnik, and the Chamber has invited the parties to make further submissions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I give Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- some information as well, which I'm sure -- Mr. Krajisnik has written a further letter, which he informs me was delivered, as far as he can deliver it, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- at the United Nations Detention Unit at, I think, 7.00 this morning was -- was what he told me. Your Honour, it's -- if I say it's a letter of a similar nature, I just mean that in the very broadest sense. It is a letter and -- I don't know where it is, of course. Last time, Your Honour, the letter took some time to get from the United Nations Detention Unit onto the Registrar's desk, so I have no idea where it is. But I can tell Your Honour that it does express, in terms which no doubt the Trial Chamber will again need to interpret and evaluate, Mr. Krajisnik's decisions in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that at least the position of Mr. Krajisnik has not changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I said it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the position has not changed. When I say that, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be my submission, Your Honour. But then my submission to Mr. Krajisnik's position was different from the Trial Chamber's view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "A letter of a similar nature, in the very broadest sense."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that was designed -- Your Honour, what I didn't want to do was start immediately making submissions as to the effect of that letter. Perhaps the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's be -- is it still the wish of Mr. Krajisnik - and I could address you directly, Mr. Krajisnik - is it still your wish to defend yourself? I mean, that's the basic matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one thing I can do, which is I do have a copy of the letter, and it would be possible - I'm not trying to stifle Mr. Krajisnik again, of course, or indeed trespass on the Trial Chamber - but just to say that Mr. Krajisnik has very kindly given me a copy of the letter. It's in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is a very simple matter to let the Trial Chamber know what is the content of the letter rather than me simply describe it as similar in broad terms in a rather lengthy manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first ask Mr. Krajisnik whether the basis of his decision is the same. That's a simple question, Mr. Krajisnik, whether it's still your wish to defend yourself and not to be assisted by counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already mentioned in my first letter, I reached that decision unwillingly, the decision to defend myself. And what I said then, I repeated in my second letter, and I don't really think that anything has changed since. If you need any additional information, I'm available to provide it to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your basic position is the same. We could do two things. If the letter is very long, perhaps we should wait until the moment that we have seen. If it's a short letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It isn't long, Your Honour. I could tell Your Honour that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's a short letter, we could ask someone to read it so that at least everyone in this courtroom is aware of what position exactly you've taken. If it would be read. Mr. Krajisnik, why not for you to do it yourself, if you have a copy, or if Mr. Stewart would provide you with a copy? And as you know, Mr. Krajisnik, while reading speed goes up usually. So for the interpreters - I see you have a copy - could you please slowly read your letter so that we're aware of the content.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I keep objecting to people speaking too fast, but when one has to speak oneself, one often doesn't realise that it's too fast. But I'll do my best. "Subject: The visit of the representative of the Registry. To: The Registry of The Hague Tribunal. Since the discussion was held in court on Wednesday, the 25th of May, 2005" -- no, I didn't say 2005 -- "I have met with Mr. van der Vliet and Mr. Petrov from the Registry of The Hague Tribunal. On that occasion, I confirmed that, although unwillingly, I was determined in my decision to take over my own defence. I wished the Registry and/or the Trial Chamber to provide me with information as to what sort of assistance and support would be available to me in the course of conducting my own defence. "The Registry representatives on that occasion informed me that they were not ready to provide answers to my questions. They needed more time to consider the matter, and they were expecting to be able to answer those questions soon. However, I would just like to clarify that I do need this information now as of consequence of my decision and not in order for me to be able to make this decision. I also explained to them that my decision is not conditional in any way and that since last Wednesday I was indeed in a position to consider my position from every point of view, and this is my firm and well-considered decision. Furthermore, I told the Registry representatives in some detail what the reasons for my decision are. I informed them that I would present those arguments to the Trial Chamber on the occasion of the upcoming Status Conference. Best regards, Momcilo Krajisnik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik, so that we are aware of the content of your letter. But first of all, Madam Registrar, in view of the submissions made by the Registry today, if anyone from the Registry would be present during this hearing, especially since they offered further explanations on the matters raised, could you inform them that they're welcome to join this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I offer just two small points on that letter. First of all, I think Mr. Krajisnik simply had difficulty with the pronunciation. The two gentlemen he refers to are Mr. van der Vliet and Mr. Petrov, Mr. van der Vleit, of course, being the chief of OLAD. I don't think there's any issue about that. And the second point, a slightly different one, Your Honour, is that my -- I've got a double-strong B/C/S team today. I am informed, it's suggested that the word, which is "nerado", which came across as "unwillingly," that the sense is "reluctantly". But, Your Honour, of course I can only ever -- I can't comment on the Serbian half of anything. But that's just the information that I'm getting, that that's the sense of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps we could just ask you for an explanation. Although I'm not a native English speaker, I do understand that "unwillingly" means that you would want to do something else than you do; whereas, "reluctantly" means that you regret that you have to do it. If this is sufficiently explaining the difference -- Mr. Stewart, I'm looking to you or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the trouble is, I wouldn't - with the greatest respect, Your Honour - I wouldn't be 100 per cent happy about the explanation in English, but Mr. Karganovic is even more unhappy, if that's possible, about the way that it's coming across in Serbian, which, or course, is not Your Honour's bit of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's say that, Mr. Krajisnik, whatever exactly the word is, that you have not whole-heartedly have chosen this position. That's at least it's putting it in a different way, and let's leave the details, for the time being, apart. I now first turn to the Prosecution. We have received a rather lengthy submission this morning. Mr. Stewart, you've been able to read it. Mr. Krajisnik, are you aware, approximately, of the submission of the Prosecution, what it is about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me, then, try to briefly explain that to you. The Prosecution submission analyses from a legal point of view the basis and the limits of the right of self-representation, and gives this analysis on the basis of texts, such as the text of the Statute, on the basis of the case law, both in this Tribunal but also in new tribunals, such as the Special Court of Sierra Leone. But apart from the case law of these international tribunals, the submission also pays quite some attention to case law developed in various countries, including the former Yugoslavia, including England, France, Germany, United States. So many, many countries are covered by these submissions, and it gives a further legal analysis of the problem. This is just for your explanation. Finally, the submission pays quite some attention to the conditions under which imposed counsel, duty counsel, and standby counsel would have to work, at least, how these conditions are formulated, and it also pays some attention to the practice of these different phenomena in the various countries. Mr. Harmon, is this a fair summary of what your submissions contain?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In addition to which, it also focuses upon the nature of the inquiry that must be made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- by the Chamber in order to determine the issue of whether Mr. Krajisnik should represent himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A request for urgent translation of that submission has been issued. Then, Mr. Harmon, I would say that in view of the lengthy submission, especially on the subjects the Chamber invited the parties to make submissions on, I suggest that we first now give an opportunity to the Defence to clarify its position, and that would mean, Mr. Stewart, you first, and then I'll give an opportunity to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just help myself to a different lectern from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'd like to do to start with is - and it's not in a sense a direct response, though of course I do have comments to make in relation to the Prosecution's submissions - is to indicate to Your Honours how we submit - we in this situation has really just got to be we, the counsel, Ms. Loukas and I - the way we submit the Statute, the Rules, and the assignment directive actually work. Because in our submission, the Registry is wrong about one critical element in its submission. We've only very recently seen the Registry's submission, but what we do see in it, unless we completely misunderstood it, is the contention that the Registrar's approval for withdrawal of assigned counsel is always required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that the Defence takes the position that the announcement of Mr. Krajisnik to defend himself would have as a consequence that there's no need to withdraw you any more because it follows from the text itself that you will then not continue to act as counsel for Mr. Krajisnik? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, from the fact that I mention it immediately, you may conclude that it has not remained unnoticed, this great difference. If there's any need to -- if you'd like to give further arguments for that, but I think the position is quite clear, and I noticed it in the submission made by the Registry, that they still have to take a decision. In your view, they will certainly not have to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I need develop the matter no further if the Trial Chamber is going to say that it accepts our submissions and that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it accepts it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I just say that the difference of you is perfectly clear. So there's no need to explain the difference of you any more. But if you, of course, would like to support your view, then of course you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes. Well, that's clear, then. Yes, well, indeed I would. Thank you. Your Honour, the starting point -- and we needn't dwell on that. The starting point, and that's well established, is that 21(4)(D) of the Statute contains what, in accordance with the Milosevic Appeals Chamber decision, is a presumptive but not inviolable right to represent yourself. Your Honours, Rule 45(A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence provide for the assignment of counsel to an accused who lacks means, and then expressly that's to be in accordance with procedure established in a directive, which one assumes was in contemplation at the time that Rule was drafted but is -- is now in existence as, what I'll call, the assignment directive, the directive on assignment of counsel. Your Honour, the terms of that directive are important and do require careful attention, with respect, Your Honour. The way in which it works is this: That Article 20 of that directive - and do Your Honours have that conveniently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't say that I know it by heart, but I thoroughly studied it, and the same is true for the rest of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was wondering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I've got it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- whether Your Honours had it available in front of you, because it is, after all, a text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we are going to be looking at inevitably some quite detail of wording, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So 20(A), "Replacement of Counsel." "Where the assignment of counsel is withdrawn by the Registrar or where the services of assigned counsel are discontinued, the counsel assigned" -- and then it goes on to place some limits on the circumstances in which counsel may immediately withdraw from acting. But, Your Honour, the distinction is drawn there right at the very beginning between assignment of counsel withdrawn by the Registrar and services of assigned counsel being discontinued. And they are clearly different or, as a matter of obvious construction, there would be no reference to the second, the discontinuance of services. If assignment always needed to be withdrawn by the Registrar and if assignment -- if withdrawal of assignment by the Registrar was required to follow in order to implement, ratify, or allow effect to be given to the discontinuance of the services of assigned counsel, there wouldn't have been any reference there to the second limb. It simply wouldn't have been necessary. The article would have just said "where the assignment of counsel is withdrawn by the Registrar." Enough. Because if that were all that was required, that is all that would need to be said. So they clearly are different. Your Honour, there is no provision, and we don't assert that there is any provision in these Articles or in the Rules expressly or by implication which would allow assigned counsel themselves or him or herself simply to discontinue. It's not open to me as lead counsel, Ms. Loukas, it's not open to us to say, "We discontinue our services. We are resigning." That -- we acknowledge that's clear. Discontinuance applies to the client sacking counsel. And I use that colloquial word because that clearly expresses the position, that's what it applies to. It actually can't apply to anything else. Withdrawal and suspension are clearly different for a start. We can get "suspension" out of the way. That's another term that appears in the Rules. But if we look at Article 19, suspension and withdrawl of counsel, 19(B) provides for particular circumstances in which suspension may occur. Pretty rare, although not in this particular case, as it happens. But we can put that on one side. Of the two possibilities that are then contemplated by Article 20, withdrawal by the Registrar, on the one hand, discontinuance by the client, sacking of counsel, on the other. Withdrawal by the Registrar can arise in a number of specified circumstances. One which we need to just look at, but in order to eliminate in effect but for understanding along the way, is Article 18. Article 18 provides that "Assignment of counsel may be withdrawn if" -- and I can summarise: The client comes into money, first; or secondly, more assets come to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, the irrelevant options need no discussion. It's clear that that's not the case. They need no attention at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mention them only because they are part of the scheme. So a few seconds pointing to the ones that don't actually apply are nevertheless necessary, Your Honour, to give a clear indication of what the scheme is of these Rules, and that's what I'm doing. But that's done, Your Honour. That's one of the situations. Article 19, then, is the only other Article which provides for withdrawal of counsel, because we've eliminated suspension. And that provides for discretionary withdrawal under 19(A), which is subject to -- for present purposes, it probably doesn't matter, Your Honour, whether I describe it as a judicial or a quasi-judicial determination by the Registrar. The concept is clear enough either way. It's not just an administrative decision. And we know that because it says so expressly in 19(F), it's subject to review by the Registrar, and the principles of review make it clear that it's a judicial or quasi-judicial decision. So there's discretionary withdrawl under 19(A), and that's the one that has to be operated, for example, if counsel wishes to withdraw, counsel wishes to take the initiative. There is also mandatory withdrawal under 19 -- sorry, under 19(C), "The Registrar shall withdraw the assignment of counsel," and then in a number of specified circumstances Counsel ceases to be eligible to appear in front of the Tribunal or is held in contempt of Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I take it that the reference to 19(F) your saying that it's reviewed by the Registrar was a slip of the tongue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 19(F), Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Review by the President or by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what did I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, that was a slip of the tongue. Yes, Your Honour is completely right there. Of course, review by the President of the Tribunal. Of course, thank you. What is of note, then, is that under 19(E), however counsel is withdrawn or under -- whichever route under Article 19, "The Registrar shall immediately assign a new counsel to the suspect or accused." So the point there under that mechanism -- it's different from 18. 18 is because -- and it was necessary to mention 18 for that reason. 18 is where, essentially, the accused has become ineligible to have assigned counsel because he can pay for it. He doesn't qualify as indigent. So that's why 18, then, doesn't contain a similar provision for immediate replacement. But in whatever circumstances, whether it's the discretionary withdrawal or the mandatory withdrawal of assigned counsel, under (E), the Registrar, mandatory again, shall immediately assign a new counsel. Moving back on to Article 20, the point is that where the assignment, the two limbs, if you like, of 20(A), where the assignment of counsel is withdrawn by the Registrar, it's either under Article 18, as I've said, where a question of replacement doesn't arise because the accused can afford it and if he's going to have counsel, he's going to have to pay for his own counsel, so there's no longer going to be assigned counsel, or it's going to be, under Article 19. In that case, Article 19, there must be a replacement. That's in contra-distinction to the other possibility, which is the one that applies here, where the services of assigned counsel have been discontinued. And the structure, then, of 20(A) is very clear, and the demonstration of the difference between withdrawal and discontinuance is illustrated and confirmed by the rest of 20(A), which then says what is going to happen by way of -- or what can happen by way of withdrawal from acting. It's perfectly clear that withdrawal from acting is a different concept from withdrawal by the Registrar. The word "withdraw" in the English version appears in both places. But we are clearly talking about two different things because "withdrawal from acting" follows "withdrawal by the Registrar", with a suspension of withdrawal from acting for a period in specified circumstances after, by definition, the Registrar has already withdrawn the assignment. And the way in which Article 20 works, in terms of what is contemplated, is that, in the case of a withdrawal by the Registrar, under Article 19 - ignore 18 - in the case of withdrawal by the Registrar under Article 19, a replacement counsel must be provided by the Registrar, under 19(E), but until that has happened, the withdrawn counsel must continue acting. So it covers that interim period. In the case of withdrawal under Article 18, of course there's no longer any entitlement to assigned counsel. The Registrar doesn't have to provide a replacement. Where the services of counsel have been discontinued - so that's the other limb and the other concept expressly contemplated by Article 20(A) - counsel must continue and not withdraw from acting. Counsel will not have been withdrawn. Counsel will have had services discontinued but cannot withdraw from acting until either the accused declares his intention in writing to conduct his own defence or provides, which means pays for, replacement counsel because the wording does cover that. "Counsel assigned may not withdraw," which is Ms. Loukas and me, well, it's me as lead counsel, "may not withdraw from acting until either replacement counsel" -- oh, I'm sorry, "either replacement counsel have been provided by the Tribunal," that's not been supplied, "or by the suspect or accused." So if Mr. Krajisnik were himself, out of his own money, to appoint another counsel, then, of course, he wouldn't be then declaring his intention to represent himself in writing. But it is at that point that I could then withdraw from acting, but I would have to wait -- if Mr. Krajisnik were not intending to represent himself, I would have to wait until Mr. Krajisnik had, out of his own pocket, appointed a replacement counsel. But that's not the situation. We got the situation clearly contemplated by Article 20, which is "Services of assigned counsel are discontinued." The only hiatus, if you like, or the only suspension of that coming into operation, in terms of my withdrawing from acting, is until he declares his intention in writing to conduct his own defence. Well, since he does that and has done that by the same document at the same time, so the discontinuance of my services - and Ms. Loukas's with them - but the discontinuance of my services and the declaration of his intention in writing to conduct his own defence come in the same document. There isn't any room for that delay. So my withdrawal from acting happens immediately. Now, Your Honour, the only way in which that can not have operated is if, notwithstanding the express and unequivocal terms in which Mr. Krajisnik expresses his letter as a man of whom no possible suggestion is made that he is not an adult man in full possession of his faculties, the only way in which that can be said not to have happened is if on examination -- and, Your Honour, we do not deny and suggest that it isn't the responsibility of the Tribunal conscientiously to explore to the point of being satisfied that an adult male in -- well, it doesn't matter whether he's male, but Mr. Krajisnik is, of course, as an adult in possession of his faculties, isn't under some serious error or misconception, something that would actually vitiate the action. But in our submission, I won't develop that for the moment, Your Honour. That's perhaps another fairly large topic here. But it would be our basic submission that it would take a lot to vitiate a conscious decision of an adult intelligent, educated man such as Mr. Krajisnik, who has seen this trial developing around him over this period. But that's perhaps an issue to be considered in due course. But as far as the operation of Article 20 is concerned, unless it is held that on such examination there is something to vitiate the plain terms of Mr. Krajisnik's letter - and I'm now talking about his recent letter, without resiling from the submissions we made in relation to the earlier letter - unless there is something to vitiate that letter, this has already happened, and our services have been discontinued. There has been no room for operation -- to the very most a scintilla of time perhaps in theory, but there has been no room for operation of the hiatus or the suspension of our withdrawal from acting. Our services have been discontinued. The Registrar has no role in this, in the sense that his approval is not required. There does not need to be withdrawal. This is another strand altogether; this has happened. So the only areas or exploration -- well, I say they're the only, Your Honour, one could -- people can always come up with other areas for exploration. But the only areas of substance or key areas for exploration here are the possible - and I say no more than that - the possible invalidity of Mr. Krajisnik's decision on the basis that there is something that would vitiate it, about which I've just expressed our position in a nutshell. We've not developed that submission, or different strand, different possibility altogether, which is the one -- or is something developed in the Prosecution's submissions, which is the possibility that in the particular circumstances of this case, either now or at some future point in the light of how the matter develops, the Court might consider it appropriate to appoint standby counsel as the convenient label, but counsel of the type - although each case has to then adjust to its own particular facts and circumstances - of the type appointed in Mr. Milosevic's case. But that comes – logically, that is there as a possibility, of course. There is absolutely nothing to prevent that exploration, but logically it comes after what, unless there is a vitiation of Mr. Krajisnik's expressed decision, after what has already happened, the discontinuance of our services and our withdrawal from acting. And Your Honour, a point which reinforces what we said in any case are crystal clear from these Rules and the assignment, is that you must remember that Mr. Krajisnik -- the assignment of counsel to Mr. Krajisnik has not been - and we know this, of course, from lots of other matters explored in the case - has not been on the basis that we and the Defence team that goes with us are entirely paid for by the Tribunal, because they're not. Mr. Krajisnik is required to contribute a substantial portion of that. It doesn't matter what it is, Your Honour, for present public purposes. The Trial Chamber knows perfectly well what it is. It's probably been discussed in public. Anyway, it doesn't matter. Your Honours know there's a -- it's a significant amount of money. It's a significant amount of money monthly, and it's a significant amount of money in total. That is another reason. As a matter of the rationale and also on the Rules, that is another reason why a client, an accused in Mr. Krajisnik's position, is in fact free to discontinue the services of assigned counsel. Because otherwise, as long as assigned counsel continues, he continues under that obligation to contribute a substantial sum of money monthly, gradually working towards -- because Your Honours know the way it's done is, a total is assessed of what he can and should contribute, and then it's divided up by the projected months of the trial. So, in fact, it's a very substantial lump sum which he is required to make as a contribution. And a defendant in Mr. Krajisnik's position is, of course, entitled and must be entitled to say, Well, I don't want to do that, thank you very much. I don't want to be under this obligation. I don't want to have a defence through assigned counsel which either has to be done on short rations, has to be done with less funds than are deemed to be necessary by the Registry, or I have to pay my money. He is entitled to choose not to do that, and we don't need to explore the reasons, and we don't need to explore whether, in fact, that forms any part of Mr. Krajisnik's reasoning. That's not the point. It is quite clear, as a matter of principle, that he must be entitled to do that. And that fits the Rules. There is, we submit, unless - and we accept that in principle though the facts are another matter - unless his letter and his decision can be set aside as not a valid decision, in which case none of this arises. I acknowledge that. If it isn't -- if it isn't really a decision of an adult person, then it -- none of it has any effect. Then his letter is just not worth the paper it's written on. But once you get beyond that step, it is perfectly clear under the Rules that he has discontinued our services, and the alternative, which is that he's compulsorily to have retained us, is first of all inconsistent with the Rules, clearly inconsistent with what under the terms of the Rules has plainly already happened, and is also inconsistent with his right to say, No, I don't wish to keep on paying my money to have assigned counsel. I want to defend myself, thank you very much. So, Your Honour, that's the starting point. That's not, of course, everything we'd have to say, because there -- there are our submissions in relation to the Prosecution's submissions. But it may be that the right course there is for the -- it's not a criticism, Your Honour, but in view of the time frame in which this material has arrived, it may be that the right course, then, is for the Prosecution to develop their submissions, as far as they wish to. And I see that Mr. van de Vliet from the Registry -- good afternoon. Mr. van de Vliet is here, as well, and no doubt they would wish the opportunity, as well. And then the Defence could deal with those other matters so far as they arise. I hope that's helpful, anyway, Your Honours, to set out what the Defence thinks is the scheme and the way it works and the reason why we -- we start from the position that we are gone, as Mr. Krajisnik's counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could ask some comments from Mr. van de Vliet on this point. We just have read your submissions by the Registry, which seem to take the starting point that a decision still has to be taken on withdrawal. Whereas, Mr. Stewart has explained to us, and I just speak for myself, not entirely unexpectedly, that the system is that if for any of the reasons mentioned in Article 18 or Article 19 of the directive on assignment of Defence counsel, that there we would have a situation that the Registrar takes a decision. But where the accused informs the Registry that he has elected to conduct his own defence, notifying them in accordance with Rule 45(F), that then on the basis of Article 20, where no replacement is needed because the accused says, I don't want to be represented any more, I want to conduct my own defence, that there there's no decision needed any more from the Registrar. Could you, since you have taken a different view, although it might not at this moment have much effect because you say the decision is delayed anyhow, but could you give us your view on the position taken by the Defence and why, on the basis of the text of especially 18, 19, and 20 of the directive, you would consider that the Registrar still would have to take a decision. MR. VAN DE VLIET: Sure, Your Honours. Thank you. I am pleased to be here on behalf of the Registry. Just a few words in explanation. I think the position of the Registry has been that it's eventually up to the Trial Chamber to decide on the request of the accused to represent himself. And while the decision of the Registry depends on the interests of justice, it would be premature for the Registrar to take any decision on that basis, thereby prejudging perhaps the outcome that you would like to take and the position that you would like to take on the matter of self-representation itself. And it's basically based on Article 19(A). We see the Article 20 as a follow-up provision to the former article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say Article 19. MR. VAN DER FLIET: Sorry, yeah. We understand a request for self-representation to also include a request for withdrawal of counsel, lead counsel at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the Defence takes the position that there's no need to ask for such withdrawal anymore, because if Mr. Krajisnik has chosen to be represented, that this discontinues the functioning of his counsel. And, of course, it's your interpretation of the letter; although it doesn't say so. I think there's no request for withdrawal. Is there anything in the text of 19 that would give support to your position? MR. VAN DER FLIET: Well, Article 19 says: "In the interest of justice, the Registrar may at the request of the accused or his counsel withdraw the assignment of counsel."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. VAN DER FLIET: So we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a request of the accused? MR. VAN DER FLIET: Yes. We have interpreted the request for self-representation to be a request for the withdrawal of the lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Stewart has drawn the attention to Article 20, where a difference is made between "withdrawal" and "the discontinuation," where he took the position that counsel may not withdraw from acting until, as it reads, that means that: "Counsel may withdraw from acting if the accused has declared his intention in writing to conduct his own defence." So they interpret Rule 20 as saying that they could immediately stop once there has been a validly-made declaration of this intention. MR. VAN DER FLIET: Yes, we have a slightly different interpretation there on Rule -- Article 20, which, in our view, could, of course, have been drafted slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if Rules would have been different, Mr. van der Vliet, then -- MR. VAN DER VLIET: Yes. As it has been drafted right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. VAN DE VLIET: But it requires a Registry act, in our view, since we have assigned counsel, as well, to withdraw him. However, the more overriding question is whether this Chamber wants to accept the request for self-representation. And we've seen it in that light, we've deferred that request to the Chamber, and I think that's the position in a nutshell of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, the Registry having clarified its position, either you still want to respond -- I mean, the difference of view is quite clear. That goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. May I respond on one single point, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- which may help for clarification. The circumstances in which the accused, in the interests of justice, under Article 19(A) may apply for withdrawal of the assignment of counsel are where he wishes to continue to have assigned counsel but wants to change them, because 19(E) makes it mandatory to have a new counsel, so that's the point. It's where he says, I'm fed up with Mr. Stewart, I want Mr. Snodgrass. That's the situation. I don't know about Mr. Snodgrass. He may be very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not speculate on the qualities of -- Mr. van der Vliet. MR. VAN DER VLIET: Yes. I understand the position of counsel to be that Article 19 is mostly meant to address the situation of a replacement of counsel, but the same could be said for Article 20 which -- the title says already "Replacement of counsel."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same time you certainly have noticed that the first part of 20(A) talks about replacement of counsel; whereas, the second part does not. MR. VAN DER VLIET: Yes. I think, as I said, I think the opinion of the Registry is that these Rules and Articles do not cover exhaustively the situation, and therefore we have made an interpretation and looked at the interest of justice itself. We thought that we couldn't make a determination as of yet because if we would do so, we would prejudge the outcome of Your Honours' decision, and therefore, we have applied Article 19(A) for the time being, awaiting your decision on the self- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. representation question itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, positions are clear. Mr. Stewart, would you like to make any further submissions, apart from these ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On this matter of the applicability of Article 19, 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The difference of view is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. On that issue, I've made all the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as the number of points in the Prosecution submissions are concerned, well, I'm in Your Honours' hands. I don't know whether the Prosecution were intending to expand or explain or supplement in any way. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, is there any need to further -- because in view of what the Chamber asked, to give a thorough analysis, especially of the legal authorities, the case law in this Tribunal, perhaps also others outside this Tribunal rely upon, I find, well, at least an analysis, a legal analysis of these authorities, is there any need to supplement that or to add to that or, to put it differently, has anything come to your mind since this morning which needs further attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. We have submitted this, and we think it's comprehensive. We, again, reiterate our conclusion in our page 1, point 3, that, we think it's very important that the Court make a thorough inquiry to absolutely assure this Court and to make sure that the record is clear that Mr. Krajisnik does waive his right to self- representation, that it is a knowing and intelligent right, that he's been advised of the consequences of such self-representation. That's where we think this hearing should be at the moment. That's what we think the Court should be focusing on at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, our position is this: I have - - well, I've had an opportunity of reading the Prosecution's submission on my return from the United Nations Detention Unit, and between then and coming to court. Your Honour will appreciate, I'm quite sure, that there would have been no possibility of the Defence being able to devote similar resources to these particular issues at this point and also be ready to deal with witnesses. It just would have been absolutely impossible, Your Honour. We can form a view as to how many hours' work goes into what is a very thorough piece of work from the Prosecution. But, Your Honour, I can give -- notwithstanding that, I have read it and I can give Your Honour the Defence submissions on a number of points which probably will indicate, then, where there isn't disagreement, possibly where there is disagreement, and where we suggest the direction of the matter should go. I hope -- would that be helpful, Your Honour? It probably wouldn't take all that long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please submit what you want to submit. And, of course, the Chamber is fully aware of what it takes to analyse these authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to do it ourselves as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. I make -- I won't enter into any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, rather not enter into speculation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- contemplation about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Other people's problems are other people's problems, with the utmost respect, Your Honour. The Defence could not possibly have done this sort of work in the time and done its other work. But, Your Honour, just going through it, paragraph 3 -- paragraph 1 and 2 are not tendentious at all. Paragraph 3. Your Honour, it isn't a prudent course for an accused to represent himself or herself in a criminal case. Mr. Krajisnik knows that's his counsel's view. It's not the point though that Prosecution recognise he nevertheless has a qualified or presumptive right to do so. The suggestion that the Trial Chamber should subject the accused to a rigorous inquiry to determine whether he's made an intelligent and knowing waiver, Your Honour, in principle, however rigorous an inquiry the Trial Chamber is prepared to spend time upon, is something that one could have no objection to. If the -- as long as the rigorous inquiry involves ultimately the recognition that it is the right of - with the very limited qualifications which are recognized - it is the right of an accused even if the Trial Chamber and objectively other people may consider it's even a foolish thing to do. And that is very well recognised in footnote 5 -- or the text of footnote 5 in the passage cited from the Milosevic case on the next page, page 3 of the -- well, two pages on in this very document, the passage ends: "Defendants before this Tribunal then have the presumptive right to represent themselves notwithstanding a Trial Chamber's judgement that they would be better off if represented by counsel." And it could easily be that the Trial Chamber's judgement is widely shared, but it isn't the point. The passage there is part of the passage introduced with the correct contention, as exemplified in the Milosevic decision, that it is a fundamental right not to be interfered with lightly and that his right to conduct his own defence should not be disproportionately restricted. But, Your Honour, an inquiry -- nobody in principle can object to an inquiry. It produces information, one supposes. The -- there is no question here of -- this is largely acknowledged. Mr. Krajisnik is not involved in the sort of disruptive behaviour which leads the Court to take a -- a view on such matters. He is, as is recognised in -- on the face of it, good health. He is strong and robust; he is willing to continue his defence. The -- his lack of legal training is referred to. These are considerations. But the Trial Chamber may feel in relation to 8 and 9 that defendants with legal training sometimes can be even more of a menace than defendants without legal training when they come to represent themselves. There isn't perhaps a great deal in that. It's implicit and inherent in the fact that there is the right for the defendant to represent himself. After all, it's not assumed that defendants are going to be qualified lawyers, anyway; after all, the extreme likelihood is that they won't be. So he's not holding the trial to ransom, he's not seeking to disrupt the trial. Those bases for interfering with his presumptive right to represent himself do not arise. If we take, without exploring the facts -- if we take the Milosevic case as one other case before this Trial Chamber where the Tribunal has taken -- the Trial Chamber has taken steps to qualify the right of the defendant to conduct his own case without any involvement and without any interference of counsel, it is very clear from the Milosevic case, which involves in some ways some more extreme facts than Mr. Krajisnik - for example, the obvious fact that Mr. Milosevic is not equipped at all for the rigours of regular five-day-a-week or anything remotely five-day-a-week week-in week-out trial. But the strong indications are that any qualification of any interference with Mr. Krajisnik's conduct of his own defence should be very carefully confined, because he must have the conduct of his defence with whatever assistance of counsel there might be thought to be appropriate by the Trial Chamber. So, Your Honour, we suggest that the way ahead is this: Is that in the first place, it is legitimate, it is proper for the Trial Chamber at least to explore with Mr. Krajisnik, to satisfy itself that his decision is what it plainly appears to be on its face, which is a considered decision by a man who is in full possession of his faculties, and should be accepted as his decision. There is, then, in principle, no reason why the Trial Chamber should not consider, either immediately or in the light of experience and perhaps quite shortly as Mr. Krajisnik proceeds in the conduct of his own defence, whether standby counsel is appropriate and what the role of that standby counsel should be. It would be unrealistic to suggest that that is not at least a question which should be seriously considered. So to that extent, whatever the ultimate result to that extent, we are also in agreement with the Prosecution as to what the approach should be. So, Your Honour, without it being necessary this afternoon, then, perhaps for us to go into more detail in relation to the Prosecution's submissions, because those matters would probably lie beyond these first steps being taken, that we'd reserve the position in relation to that and, of course, we will have had the opportunity to give the matter fuller and more mature consideration. But those steps, exploration to be satisfied that the decision stands as a decision, in which case the consequences are, as we have submitted to the Trial Chamber this afternoon, in accordance with the Statute, Rules, and directive. And then the open question as to whether it is nevertheless appropriate for there to be some involvement of counsel, whether the word is as a supplement, or a complement, or as a support or assistance in some way to go together in accordance with the principles expounded in the Milosevic decision, with Mr. Krajisnik's conduct of his own defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The expectation is there, Mr. Stewart and Mr. Krajisnik, that the Prosecution's submissions' translation could be expected by approximately the 7th of June. That would be a week approximately. It's an extensive -- it's for your information, Mr. Krajisnik. Before we proceed and see whether the Chamber has any questions for you, I think it's the proper time for a break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to give you an opportunity to make further submissions, that could be also further explanations, of why you have expressed your intent to defend yourself, and it could be on any of the legal matters that were raised as well. So you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, allow me to thank the Trial Chamber, and I'd like to try and speak as slowly as possible in order to assist the interpreters in their work. Earlier on I listened to what the legal experts had to say, the Prosecution and others who, in an almost alarming way, have seemed to indicate that I should examine my own mind and see why I have made such a decision. If this is reported in Yugoslavia -- or rather, in Serb lands, they're going to say, All witnesses tend to say that Krajisnik was a good and intelligent man. Why, what has happened to him there if he needs to be examined, to have his head examined now? So, therefore, I would like to appeal to the Trial Chamber. It would be a good idea if I could explain to you the reasons underpinning my decision because throughout my life I've always tried to participate in the search for solutions and not decisions. Because anyone alive could say, How come he reached such a decision now? He could have done it in the beginning. In the beginning, he opted for a Defence team, for the services of a lawyer. And you yourselves must find this rather odd as well. Since Judge Orie is a strict and just Judge and whenever he stops somebody in their flow, they tend to forget their name let alone anything else -- I mean, I would really like to appeal to you to provide me with the opportunity to speak out and have the opportunity to say and to explain to you why I was not in a position to simply look for a solution, but to make a decision. I had to make a decision. The first reason why I reached this decision to conduct my own defence -- well, I'd like to explain to you what I meant when I said "reluctantly or unwillingly." This is a specific Serb expression. I do admit that it would be better to have the services of a lawyer rather than to conduct my own defence. It's their job, after all. I wanted to study law, then I studied economics. And so I'm not a lawyer myself. So how come I've reached this decision? It has to do with a number of reasons. I tried to participate in the search for solutions. First of all, one of the first reasons I've opted for this decision is my Defence counsel, Mr. Stewart. We have many points in common, and I said, Well, God forbid if I had to be his lawyer. I mean, our natures are somehow similar, and we often argue, but that's not the reason why I've reached this decision. I've decided along the lines of what was said by Mr. Stewart and Ms. Loukas. They said, We're not in a position to properly defend Mr. Krajisnik. Now, a solution has to be found; we can't postpone this. I mean, if they're in a position to say, Okay, now we're ready to do it properly -- if you will have the kindness to listen to me. I mean, I can't tell you what he should have done, I'm not that intelligent, but I do have some idea where I think what he should have done. The second reason: Gentlemen, Your Honours, at this court, through no one's particular doing but some people are really to blame for this -- but there are witnesses who don't tell the truth. We have three categories of witnesses, according to me, some who are not even aware of the fact that they're telling lies because they got their information through the media or in some other ways. I did mention one person, if you remember, even before this Trial Chamber started its work, and this person is likely to come back here. The second category of witness being cross-examined by the Prosecution are witnesses who in some way have a kind of phobia. They're scared, and they're trying to second-guess what the Prosecution wants them to say. My Defence counsel, without any offence, I think he's a good lawyer, but let me make a comparison nevertheless. He's a good soccer player who never scores. There are lots of obstacles in his way, but he never scores. He wasted four years. I mean, all this time had been taken up by others, and he can't really make up for lost time, and therefore he can't even begin to know what a Bjelobrk or someone else might be all about. And therefore I've made the suggestion -- I've made this proposal to actively participate in my own defence. The third reason: Gentlemen, Your Honours, I am a man who has always tried not to cause offence or insult anyone. If you comb through all the papers, you will never hear any references to my calling Muslims by any names. And then my Defence said, Oh, Krajisnik said, are those Turks? And then they said, Oh, yes, you have said that. And it was a discussion between Karadzic and myself. And I said, Do you have Turks visiting you? And he said, No, I've got Tunisians there. But this is not the kind of language I use. I don't want to cause offence. And also, with all due respect, one of the reasons behind my decision is the Trial Chamber. When I was supposed to select my lawyer, I do have relatives who are refugees here in Holland, in Leiden. And I said, Who do you suggest? Do you have an idea? And they said, there is a very good lawyer who is very familiar with our circumstances, and they showed me the picture, and it said: "Lawyer Alphons Orie." And I was enthusiastic, and I said, Well, what is he like? And they said, He spends 24 hours a day working. He only wants to establish the truth. And I said, Well, that's what I need, the guy who is going to look for the truth. And then I realised that it was the same picture, only the colour of your hair was slightly different. And you will remember how pleased I was when you asked the question about the prior Trial Chamber. I wanted to make a gift to the previous Judge, El Mahdi, and then there was a new Judge, and I saw that there was something else, a different approach, a different way of establishing the truth, and then I said, Who is the new Judge? Because I was interested, of course. And I was told, You are a lucky man, indeed, almost as if God has protected you. This person is never going to be made to do anything which runs counter to the truth. All he wants to do is to establish the truth and the whole truth. And then I wondered what it was all about. And then I saw that we had witnesses here telling lies, and then I said to myself, I really don't want to act against my own interests. I want to defend myself. I want to successfully defend myself. My lawyer feels that I should be defended, but I feel I should be defended successfully. So there is a difference between the Serb and the English approach. And when the trial first started, I told Judge Canivell,I'm not guilty, but I'm not asking you to take my word for it. Just enable me to establish the truth, and I'm 100 per cent certain that it can be done if the truth is told. Today, and my lawyer knows that, this sort of excellent lawyer I've got is actually an obstacle to me, and we've got a great representative from the Registry here as well. And I said, Well, I've got quite a few tapes. Could I have a filing cabinet and something that I could put my binders and everything in? And they said, No, no, no, no. You've got a lawyer. He can deal with this. And I have to, you know, have my stuff all over the place in my cell because I've got a lawyer and he's supposed to take care of it. Now, another problem between Mr. Stewart and myself -- I don't know whether he's to blame or the Registry is to blame, it will be up to you to decide. I don't know if you remember, gentlemen, the Registry decided that I could participate in my own defence, and they made that decision and said, We have reached the decision to provide funds for a counsel and a co-counsel and the rest must be co-financed. And I said, I have no funds. And they showed me the figure that was spent on my case for the people who were there before, and it is an enormous amount. And then I asked for a lawyer, and whoever I asked for, everybody said, I don't want to defend you. The pay is not good enough. How the Registry managed to convince Mr. Stewart to take up my cause, I really have no idea. All of a sudden they came along and said, Mr. Stewart agreed to do the job for this amount of money. And then I was obviously in prison and already at that stage I have told you I had no money, and I believe that Jovanovic, who did his expertise - and I'm not going to waste another word on him, and I've already said quite a bit of bad things about him, which is not a good thing in itself - but I believe I must do my best in order to make funds available for an investigator. And my Defence counsel knows this. You can't make bread unless you have flour. I mean, investigators must do their work in the field, and this is something else I've mentioned here before. My witnesses, I mean, for example, we couldn't get certain witnesses to come here but the Prosecution managed to convince them to come here. I don't know. They make statements and submit them to the Prosecution but not to us. Actually, I know the reasons, but it doesn't matter. And when I said that half of our witnesses are hiding around in forests and are too scared to come, I mean, there is a court in Sarajevo and those people who have made statements are doing their best to avoid this because they're afraid to go to Sarajevo. Perhaps through their witnesses, whilst tendering documents we could already prove what is the truth of the matter and make the whole story shorter, because these people are not going to be brought here that easily. And also, our witnesses tend to tell tales and they never actually refer to the situation the way it is. And since we can't get any witnesses, I am asking for a decision to be made in the Republika Srpska, and they should commit themselves to helping us out, find witnesses in the same way they're helping the Prosecution. And I have to apologise here. I was fully in favour of starting the whole trial from scratch because in the meantime, until the break, we came up with quite a few new documents. But time has passed, et cetera, and we could have proved, okay, this is a document which proves whether Mr. Krajisnik was present on such-and-such an occasion or not. That was my main aim, not to prolong matters in any way. And also, coming back to these funds and resources, the decision was made, and I disagree with that decision because I don't think it's the right one but I respect it anyway, the decision on resources. No resources left. Okay. And in the same way I respect the decision that we can't have any extra time. But when it comes to resources, which were actually made available afterwards, they must be spent on investigators. They must be enabled to do their job. And when we talk about resources, Mr. Stewart, I mean, has looked at all the materials, but even if he had three extra years, he would never be able to manage all that. So taking all this into consideration, I had no other way out. I mean, all things were going in a certain direction. A sentence. We have the media here. I mean, why was I in favour of private sessions all the time? Last time I mentioned that I would like an investigator who could look for people who are hiding around in forests and in woods, Karadzic and such like, and my investigators said, No, no, no, we can't look for anyone. SFOR is going to pick us up. I was not in favour of that. I was in favour of looking for people who might be scared. You did have one witness here who was clearly frightened, and I just wanted to get these people to come here in order to speed things up and be done with it. And perhaps the Registry is not going to admit this, but it was quite clear that my request has put them in a difficult situation. He wants to defend himself. How are we going to cope with that? And it is a problem for the Trial Chamber as well. Now I'm asking for all these documents and materials, so I'm causing problems and difficulties to everyone, and first and foremost to myself, because I could not find any other solution. How can I make sure that I get a just and fair defence? And perhaps the representative of the Registry could confirm this. I said, I am always going to accept a better solution, but a solution which will make it possible for me not just to defend myself but to defend myself successfully. I'm not some kind of scare-monger. I'm not trying to cause trouble to anyone. But my decision, believe me, is a fully pondered and considered decision, because it is quite clear I can conduct my defence much better than a Defence counsel who has, himself, admitted that he was unable to do so. But the Secretariat, or rather, the Registry is not making anything available to me. But I believe in God, I am 100 per cent certain that I am going to walk out of here a free man, because I am definitely not guilty. But I do appeal to you. I thought I would need more time today. But this is a long story, I have not actually prepared because I was preparing for the witness the whole time, and when I looked at the situation - I do apologise. I do understand people who speak too fast now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come to a conclusion, Mr. Krajisnik. We have some questions to be put to the Defence as well. And I see that you came to a point which you dealt with before, that you said that you could better defend yourself where Defence counsel admitted they could not properly do the job. So if you could please conclude in two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Repetition happens because I am not checking my notes. But just one more point and then I'll wrap it up. The documentation that we get from the Prosecution, no offence intended, because I do respect all Prosecutors and they're all good, but one of them is slightly less good. I'm not going to name any names, it doesn't really matter, but I often receive those documents too late, too late in the day, and I really do want to participate actively. And there are quite a few other points that I should mention here, but since I did say earlier on you are a fully respectable and a professional Trial Chamber -- I did not say I hoped so, but I trust that you are, and I do respect you, and I am certain that you are going to reach a just and fair decision. And as I've always tried to do, this time too I will try and allow for sufficient time in order for everyone to be able to bring up their arguments. But if there are any questions, I will be available. I don't know how prepared I'm going to be to answer those questions, but I would be glad to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I'd like to raise a few matters, legal matters. First - and that's not a legal matter, Mr. Stewart - when you suggested that once the decision as a principle would have been taken that Mr. Krajisnik would be allowed to defend himself and that then, of course, one can think about standby counsel or amicus or whatever, am I right in understanding that this was not an offer that you would be available to accept such a position if that decision would ever have been taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no, it -- the whole thing is in such a state of flux that it can't be an offer, no, and it isn't, and I can say, Your Honour, neither is it for Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's at least clear. And I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- avoid whatever doubt that could come into our minds --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I don't want to say it's an unequivocal offer that is just there for the acceptance, if I put it in those terms, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Stewart, we have seen, and not only for the first time in the submission of this morning by the Prosecution, that under almost or even complete -- literally the same text, that is, European Convention on Human Rights, the International Conference on Civil and Political Rights, the the Statute of this Tribunal, the Statute of the Rwanda Tribunal, that a totally different practice has developed in many countries. You may have noted that in quite some continental European countries under certain conditions, France, Germany, that counsel is imposed, but that may have been clear. But now the Prosecution also introduces English case law, and I'm specifically drawing your attention to the Woodward case, which I had not an opportunity yet to study carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm in exactly the same position as Your Honour. I had noted the case, but have similarly not had such an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course I hoped that, especially English case law, would be -- but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, your, I'm sorry, that's just unrealistic. We don't carry it around in our heads in that way, as I'm sure Your Honour knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We carry some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, because I would have invited you to make any comment on the lines, whether it fairly represents the decision, where it says: "Where, on the other hand, the accused makes an application to withdraw the services of his counsel in order to conduct his own defence, the judge has discretion whether to allow such an application." And a few lines further down: "The more advanced the trial, however, the less likely it is that an application to dispense with counsel's services will be successful." Whether you would have any comment on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, I can tell Your Honour exactly what I would do if I were in England or here. I would start with the assumption that's stated by conscientious counsel on the other side in their submission that was likely to be correct as far as it goes, and then would go to the case law to see exactly what it meant and how it applied and what the limits of the principle were. That, I rather apprehend, Your Honour, is the way any conscientious lawyer would work, and it's the way I would work in relation to this matter, and I would decline to make any firm submissions or comments in relation to the matter until I've taken that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. Perhaps an opportunity should still be there for you. As you may have noticed, the -- and the same question is, as a matter of fact, for the Prosecution: One of the cases on which the Appeals Chamber seems heavily to rely on is the Faretta case. This might not come as a surprise to you, Mr. Stewart, also you, Mr. Harmon. And since you explained what you usually do, that is, to carefully look at such a case, could you comment on the -- and it's perhaps a bit the same issue, at least, to some extent, it has similarity. Could you comment on the time aspect as we find it in the Faretta case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "the time aspect," Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The time aspect means: When do you say, I want counsel? When do you say, I would like to exercise my right to defend myself? Could you do that in all stages? And to that extent there might be an issue similar to the Woodward case you presented, but I have not yet studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can tell Your Honour, based on my experiences in practicing in the United States, the normal situation is that assertion that the defendant wants to represent himself tends to be made early on in the case, before it starts, at the arraignment, during the initial phases of the case. It is, in my experience, less likely to arise during the trial. The inquiries, based again on my experiences in practicing in both Federal and State Court, is that the Court, at the point where an accused makes an assertion that he wants to represent himself, then embarks on the inquiries that we have proposed be made in this case. But in answer to your question when those circumstances generally arise, generally they arise before the accused -- before the trial starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, do you have any observations? Perhaps I'll confront you with some of the language of Faretta.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where it -- although perhaps not perfectly clear what it means there, where it several times says: "Well before the date of the trial, however, Faretta requested that he be permitted to represent himself." Or a little bit further down: "Several weeks thereafter, but still prior to trial, the judge shall respond to how the hearing ..." And one of the separate opinions expresses: "The opinion of the Supreme Court leaves open a host of other procedural questions," and then some of them are mentioned. One of them being: "How soon in the criminal proceeding must a defendant decide between proceeding by counsel, or per se, must he be allowed to switch in mid-trial." And then very optimistically, a little bit further it says: "I assume that many of these questions will be answered with finality in due course." Do you have any comment on this language, where Faretta seems to be very much at the basis of the Appeals Chamber decision, and in view of the English case law, and in view of different interpretations of where the limits to the right to self-representations are, does this raise any need to make further observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, you quoted from Faretta. Do you by chance happen to have a page reference I could use?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether we have the same. Page 3, under 1, approximately fifth or sixth line says: "Well before the date of trial, however, Faretta --" And that is formerly, I think, on page 807, because there's a numbering in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's right in the beginning. Do you find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I find it, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then on that same page, the last paragraph: "Several weeks thereafter, but still prior to the trial." And the last quote I gave to you is - if these bold numbers are page numbers, then it's page 852 - and that is the -- let me just see whose opinion that exactly is. I think it's Justice Blackman, joined by the Chief Justice and Justice Rehnquist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have the passage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just asking whether this aspect -- well, perhaps not surprisingly -- perhaps very surprisingly it was Mr. Krajisnik who raised the issue, who said why I did not say it right at the beginning, and he was the only one who raised the time issue. But would there be any further observations as to this aspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know the Feretta case and I know the procedure that was -- that happened in the Feretta case. It's described early on where the judge advised Mr. Feretta clearly and made a very profound inquiry into whether he understood the rules of procedure, the rules of evidence. And I say, parenthetically, that I was quite surprised how knowledgeable this particular defendant in California was in respect of his knowledge of the motions and other elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many exceptions there are to the hearsay rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct. Having practiced in California 12 years, I was impressed with the degree of knowledge of this particular defendant. However, that didn't pass the test for the judge in California, and that right to represent himself was withdrawn. I think whether the desire is expressed before the trial starts or after the trial starts, I think the inquiry remains the same; I don't think that changes at all. I think that the Court, faced with an expression to represent oneself before the trial or after the trial, I don't see any particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Harmon, isn't it true that the Prosecution - and I'm also inviting Mr. Stewart to respond to that - has given more recent case law in which it is said that on an appeal you could not defend yourself, which is, of course, not obvious from the Sixth Amendment, on which the Faretta case has been based. I mean, it doesn't make any difference between first instance or an appeal. It may have something to do with legal complexity of issues.
